chapter: Freelancing, politics and New York clubs
title: McCarthy-era America and the Red squad
summary: He recalls watching the hearings, covering them for the Voice, Red squad ineptitude and blacklisting of Cisco Houston.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Let’s talk about the mainstream of American politics as it was changing from the HUAC [House Un-American Activities Committee] hearings in the late 1940s and then evolving to the ’50s and McCarthy and Eisenhower and all these changes. We’ve talked at a local level about your experiences writing and moving to New York and knowing these people, and then slight political intersections with Frankie Newton and these various things. How were you experiencing the large picture of the shift of American political life and repression and witch-hunt and red-baiting?

That’s it. I was about to say. We were in the era of Joe McCarthy. I remember watching those hearings on television, absolutely riveted. I would do nothing else until those hearings were over. I was covering some of that for the Village Voice. We had a

Red squad in the city. Some of them were so inept – I remember I was covering some kind of anti-war demonstration. A guy said he was a reporter from a local radio station. What was I doing there? What were my politics? I noticed the mic was upside down. The Red squad also filtered into music. When I did the show with Herridge, I also talked him into a folk-music show. I wanted to have Cisco Houston on. He was a very good folk singer. There was that message from the page to the producer. He was in Red channels, which was a way that they got people off the air. It pervaded every aspect of our culture, of our lives.
